name: iStat Menus
tagline: Menu bar system monitor for macOS: CPU, memory, disks, network, sensors, battery, all in dropdown graphs.

pricing.basis: one-time license, family pack and upgrade pricing available
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The easy 80 percent of iStat Menus is genuinely one-shottable: a SwiftUI MenuBarExtra app that polls host_statistics64, getifaddrs, statfs and IOPowerSources will give you live CPU, memory, disk and network readouts in your menu bar in an afternoon. The hard 20 percent is where Bjango actually lives: temperatures and fan speeds on Apple Silicon need private IOHIDEventSystemClient calls that coding agents routinely hallucinate, per-process attribution needs care, and the dropdown graphs are a real design job rather than a chart library call. You will also be signing and re-signing your own binary every time macOS changes its mind about entitlements. So: a useful personal monitor, yes. A replacement for a mature 15-year-old menu bar app that never jitters, never leaks, and reads sensors your Mac does not document, not in one sitting.
coreLoopDIY: A local Swift menu bar app that polls system APIs every second and shows CPU, memory, disk and network stats as text plus small sparkline graphs in a dropdown.
requirements: willingness to run an unsigned local build and re-approve it after updates
basic comfort with IOKit and Mach system call names
whatYouLose: Temperature and fan sensor readings, which are the single hardest part on Apple Silicon and the reason many people buy it
Per-process CPU, memory and network attribution in the dropdowns
GPU stats, detailed battery health and cycle history, and the weather and world clock extras
A layout that stays legible and cheap on CPU when you cram six monitors into a 13 inch menu bar
The iOS companion app for watching another Mac remotely
moatNotes: Fifteen years of chasing undocumented sensor APIs across every Mac Apple has shipped is not a feature list, it is accumulated scar tissue.
whyPeopleStillPay: It is a one-time purchase that costs less than a lunch and has never once been the thing that broke on their machine. A DIY monitor lives in your menu bar all day, which means every stutter, memory leak or post-update crash is a tax you pay personally. Paying Bjango is buying out of that maintenance contract, and for the specific case of thermals and fans you are also buying knowledge of hardware quirks you would otherwise reverse engineer yourself.
notes: Build it for the numbers you actually stare at, not all of them, and you will finish it.
prompt:
Build a macOS menu bar system monitor as a local personal app. Stack: Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI, MenuBarExtra, no third-party packages.

Project setup:
- Create a Swift Package Manager executable target named MiniStat, or an Xcode app project if you prefer; either way it must build with a single command and run as an agent app (LSUIElement true, no Dock icon, no main window).
- No accounts, no network calls, no telemetry, no analytics. There are no secrets, so there is no .env.

What to monitor, using only public system APIs:
- CPU: host_statistics64 with HOST_CPU_LOAD_INFO, compute deltas between samples for user, system, idle percentages.
- Memory: host_statistics64 with HOST_VM_INFO64 plus sysctl hw.memsize; report used, wired, compressed, free.
- Disk: statfs on / for total and free bytes.
- Network: getifaddrs with if_data byte counters, compute per-second up and down rates for the active interface.
- Battery, if present: IOPowerSources for percentage, charging state, time remaining.

UI:
- Menu bar label shows two compact live values chosen in settings, for example CPU percent and network throughput, in a monospaced digit font so it does not jitter.
- Dropdown shows one section per metric with current numbers and a 60 second sparkline drawn with SwiftUI Path from an in-memory ring buffer.
- Sampling on a 1 second timer, coalesced into a single ObservableObject; keep total CPU use of the app under 1 percent, measure it and say what you got.
- Settings via a small SwiftUI form in the dropdown: which two values appear in the menu bar, update interval, launch at login toggle using SMAppService.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt and do not fake: temperatures, fan speeds, GPU utilization, per-process breakdowns, notifications, remote monitoring, history beyond the in-memory buffer.

Deliverables: the source, a Makefile or one-line build command, and a README with the exact steps to build, run, allow the unsigned binary in System Settings, and enable launch at login. If any API you reach for is private or undocumented, stop and say so instead of guessing at symbol names.
